learning_objective: 🎯 Master the fundamental language of physics! Learn how to measure the universe accurately, calculate errors, and check formulas using dimensional analysis.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: The SI system has 7 base units (like meters for length, kilograms for mass, seconds for time). All other physical quantities (like speed or force) are derived by combining these base units.

To measure the distance to a planet, we observe it from two different positions on Earth. The shift in its apparent position against the background stars is the 'parallax angle', helping us calculate massive distances using trigonometry.

No measurement is perfect. 'Absolute error' is the difference between the true and measured value. 'Relative error' is the ratio of mean absolute error to the mean value. When adding/subtracting quantities, absolute errors add up!
These tell us how precise a measurement really is. Rule of thumb: all non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant, but leading zeros (like in 0.005) are not.

Every physical quantity can be expressed in terms of base dimensions like $[M]$ for Mass, $[L]$ for Length, and $[T]$ for Time. We use this to check if an equation is physically correct—the dimensions on both sides MUST match!

fun_activity.title: 👀 The Finger Parallax Trick
fun_activity.instructions: Hold your finger vertically in front of your face. Close your left eye and look at the background. Now open the left and close the right. Your finger 'jumps'! This apparent shift is exactly how astronomers measure distances to nearby stars.

exam_tips: 📌 Dimensional analysis is a guaranteed 3-mark question. Practice finding the dimensional formula of tricky constants like the Gravitational constant ($G$) or Planck's constant ($h$).
📌 When multiplying or dividing quantities, the maximum fractional (or percentage) errors are added together.
📌 An equation can be dimensionally correct but physically wrong (e.g., if a constant like $1/2$ is missing), but a dimensionally wrong equation is ALWAYS physically wrong.
quick_recap: ⭐ The 7 base SI units are meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela.
⭐ Dimensional formulas treat physical quantities algebraically (e.g., Velocity is $[LT^{-1}]$).
⭐ Rounding off rules matter: if the dropping digit is exactly 5, look at the preceding digit (even stays same, odd increases by 1).
